c1.label: Q1
c1.prompt: How is infrared different from the radio you used before?

A.text: It needs a clear line of sight

B.text: It carries numbers instead of names

c1.why: Infrared is light you cannot see. Put a hand or a wall in the way and the signal simply does not arrive.

c2.label: Q2
c2.prompt: Two cars run the same program. Someone presses a button on one IR remote. What happens?

C.text: Both cars obey, if both can see the remote

c2.why: There is no pairing. Any car running this program will act on any matching remote it can see.

c3.label: Q3
c3.prompt: When does the `on IR receiving` block run its blocks?
c3.why: It is an event block. It waits, and it wakes up when something is received.

r1.label: Q1
r1.prompt: The car gets Up once, and then no more signals. What does the car do?
r1.why: The drive block has no end. One press is enough to leave the wheels turning.

r2.label: Q2
r2.prompt: The car gets Up, then OK. What does the car do?
r2.why: Each press wakes the handler and only the matching branch runs. OK replaces the drive with a stop.

r3.label: Q3
r3.prompt: Someone presses Left on a real IR remote, but a person stands between the remote and the car. What happens?
r3.why: Infrared does not go through people or round corners. No line of sight means no signal.

r4.label: Q4
r4.prompt: What is the micro:bit screen doing while the car drives?

B.text: Showing a happy face the whole time

C.text: Showing a face only while a button is held

r4.why: The loop and the event handler are separate pieces. Neither waits for the other.

d1.label: Q1
d1.prompt: The student meant OK to be the stop button. Which change fixes it?

C.text: Move the block outside the handler

d1.why: The test is right and the block is wrong. OK should send the stop command.

d2.label: Q2
d2.prompt: This test sits on its own with no event block. What goes wrong?

C.text: It is checked once at start-up and never again

d2.why: A loose `if` runs once. The button press comes later, and by then nothing is asking.

b1.label: Q1
b1.prompt: You want five commands — up, down, left, right, stop. How is that program shaped?

B.text: One `on IR receiving` block holding five `if` tests

b1.why: One handler wakes on any signal; the tests inside it sort out which button it was.

b2.label: Q2
b2.prompt: Which block should the OK button run?
b2.why: Setting both speeds to 0 would also work, but the stop block says what you mean — and code that says what it means is easier to fix later.
